essays.T497:
A percent describes a change relative to a starting value. A percentage point is the simple arithmetic difference between two percentages. If an interest rate moves from four percent to five percent, it has risen by one percentage point, but by twenty-five percent in relative terms. Both statements are true, and headlines may choose the one that sounds more dramatic. The starting value is called the base, and it matters a great deal: a small base produces large percentage changes from small absolute ones. A rise from two cases to four is a hundred percent increase, yet it is two cases.

Understanding the difference matters when reading news about prices, rates, polls and risks. A claim that something doubled can mean little if it started tiny, and a claim that it rose by a few percent can be large if the base is huge. Gas prices, rents and pay are all better understood in dollars as well as in percent.

In practice, ask what the base is and whether the change is relative or absolute. Convert to actual amounts: what does a ten percent rise mean in dollars for your own spending? Be careful when percentages are chained.
essays.T498:
An average can mean different things. The mean adds all values and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when the numbers are lined up in order, with half above and half below. The mode is the most common value. The distribution describes how values are spread, whether clustered, even or lopsided, and outliers are values far from the rest. Income is a classic lopsided distribution: a few very high earners pull the mean up, so the median is usually a better picture of a typical household.

The choice matters because a reported average can mislead without being false. If a neighborhood's mean income is raised by one billionaire, the statement is true but not typical. Home prices, wealth, wages and tips are all reported in ways that depend on which average is used. For a gig worker, the mean earnings per trip and the median can differ widely if a few trips pay very well.

In practice, when you see an average, ask which kind it is and whether the median is also given. Look at the range and whether outliers exist. A single number never shows the spread, so look for percentiles or a chart.
essays.T499:
Surveys and polls ask a sample of people and use the answers to estimate what the whole group thinks. Because a sample is only part of the group, the result carries sampling error, which is stated as the margin of error. A margin of plus or minus three percentage points at the usual confidence level means that if the same poll were repeated many times, most results would fall within three points of the true value. Larger samples shrink the margin, but with diminishing returns: going from a thousand respondents to four thousand only halves it.

This matters because news stories often describe a lead of a point or two as meaningful. If the gap between two candidates is smaller than the margin of error, the poll cannot tell which is ahead. The margin also applies to each number separately, so the uncertainty on the gap between two options is larger than the stated margin.

In practice, find the sample size, the dates, the method and the margin of error. Check who was surveyed: adults, registered voters or likely voters give different results. Remember that the margin covers only random sampling error, not problems such as poor question wording, people who do not respond or an unrepresentative sample.
essays.T500:
A base rate is how often something happens in general, before taking account of any particular case. For example, the share of drivers who are in a serious crash in a year, or the share of small businesses that survive five years, or the fraction of a population that has a rare disease. Ignoring base rates is a common error: people focus on a vivid new piece of evidence and forget how rare or common the event is to begin with.

The idea matters because a test or a warning that is accurate can still be wrong most of the time when the event is rare. If a condition affects one person in a thousand, and a test wrongly flags five percent of healthy people, most positive results will be false alarms, since there are so many more healthy people than sick ones. Similarly, one dramatic news story about a crime or an accident says little about how often it happens.

In practice, when a statistic or an event alarms you, ask how often this normally occurs and compare. Look for the denominator: how many opportunities were there? A rise from a very low rate is still low.
essays.T501:
Two things are correlated when they tend to change together. Causation means that one actually produces the other. A correlation can arise because A causes B, because B causes A, because a third factor, called a confounder, drives both, or by coincidence. Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in summer, but one does not cause the other; hot weather affects both. The strongest way to establish cause is a randomized experiment, in which a researcher assigns people to groups by chance and compares outcomes. Observational studies can suggest causes, but need careful adjustment for confounders.

The distinction matters in nearly every news story about health, money and policy, where a headline says that something is linked to something else. Acting as if a link were a cause can lead to wasted effort or harm, and arguments about what a policy accomplished depend on this question.

In practice, when you see a link, ask what else might explain it, which direction the effect might run, and whether the sample is large and varied. Notice phrases like associated with or linked to, which do not claim cause. Look at whether the study was a randomized trial. Be careful with small samples and with trends picked from many comparisons, where some are bound to appear by chance.
essays.T502:
Many economic and business numbers follow regular patterns during the year. Retail sales jump in December, construction slows in winter, and employment of teachers and farm workers shifts with school and growing seasons. Seasonal adjustment is a statistical method that estimates the usual seasonal pattern and removes it, so that changes reflect underlying trends. The adjusted series is easier to compare from month to month, while the raw or unadjusted series shows what actually happened. Statistical agencies also revise earlier figures when more complete data arrive, sometimes by a meaningful amount.

This matters because reading a holiday spike or a winter slump as a change in direction leads to wrong conclusions. A fall in jobs after the holidays may be entirely expected. Preliminary numbers are based on partial responses, and revisions can change the story, which is why a single month's report is a weak basis for a strong claim.

In practice, check whether a number is seasonally adjusted, and compare unadjusted data with the same month in earlier years when you want to see actual levels. Look at a three-month or twelve-month trend. Watch for the word revised and the size of past revisions.
essays.T503:
A total tells you little until it is divided by something that puts it in proportion. Per capita means per person, and lets you compare places of different size. Per mile, per hour and per unit do the same for costs and earnings. A city with more crimes in total may have fewer per resident than a smaller one. A country with a larger economy may have a lower income per person. Unit cost is the price of one standard unit, such as the cost per ounce of a product or the cost per mile of a vehicle.

This kind of thinking matters most in your own work. A job that pays a large sum may be a poor deal once you count the hours and miles it takes. For a driver, real pay is what remains after fuel, maintenance, depreciation, insurance and taxes, divided by all the time spent working, including waiting and driving without a passenger. A trip that pays more in total can pay less per hour than a short one.

In practice, calculate your net earnings per hour and per mile, including the unpaid time and the expenses of the vehicle. The federal government publishes a standard business mileage rate that can serve as a rough benchmark for the cost per mile.
essays.T504:
Compound interest means that interest is earned on both the original amount and on interest already added, so growth builds on itself. A balance growing at a steady rate doubles in a time roughly equal to seventy-two divided by the percentage rate, a rule of thumb known as the rule of seventy-two. The same arithmetic works against borrowers: interest on unpaid credit card balances accumulates on itself. Discounting is the reverse process, finding what a future amount is worth today by reducing it according to a rate, because money available now can be invested or used. Expected value is the average outcome of an uncertain choice, found by multiplying each possible result by its probability and adding the results.

These ideas matter for savings, loans and choices that involve risk. Starting to save early has a large effect over decades. High-interest debt can grow faster than expected payments reduce it. Comparing a payment today with a promise of more later requires thinking about the rate.

In practice, compare loans by the annual percentage rate and the total repaid, not the monthly payment alone. Use the expected value to compare gambles, remembering it ignores how much a loss would hurt. A choice with a good average can still be unwise if a bad outcome would be ruinous.
essays.T505:
Insurance works by pooling risk. Many people pay small, certain premiums into a pool, and the pool pays large losses to the few who suffer them. It makes sense when a loss would be severe, relatively unlikely and beyond what you could absorb on your own, such as a serious illness, a major car crash or a house fire. Self-insuring means setting aside your own money to cover losses, which suits small, predictable costs. A deductible is the amount you pay before coverage starts, and a higher deductible usually lowers the premium. Adverse selection occurs when those most likely to claim are most likely to buy, which raises prices for everyone.

The logic matters to a self-employed person, who has no employer providing benefits. Choices include health coverage, vehicle liability and commercial coverage that applies while driving for a platform, disability income protection and renters or homeowners insurance. State law requires liability insurance for drivers in Indiana.

In practice, insure against losses that could wreck your finances, and self-insure smaller ones by keeping an emergency fund. Compare policies by the coverage limits, exclusions, deductible and premium, and read what is excluded, especially for personal policies used for paid driving. Ask an agent about gaps.
essays.T506:
Charts are persuasive, which is why they are sometimes used to mislead. Common tricks include a truncated axis, where the vertical scale starts well above zero so that a small difference looks large, especially in bar charts, where the length of the bar is supposed to represent the amount. Others include stretching or squeezing the scale, choosing a time window that begins at a convenient peak or trough, hiding the denominators by showing counts instead of rates, using two vertical axes to make unrelated lines appear to track each other, and using pictures whose area grows faster than the number they represent.

Careful reading matters because a visual impression forms in a moment and is hard to undo. Charts appear in political arguments, advertisements and financial reports, and a misleading one can persuade without containing a single false number.

In practice, look first at the axes: where does each start, what are the units, and is the spacing even? Read the title and the labels, and check the source and the date range. Ask whether a different start or end date would change the story. Check if the chart shows the whole picture, including the long-term trend, or only a selected stretch. Compare the visual size of the difference with the actual numbers.
essays.T507:
Incentives are the rewards and penalties that influence decisions, and a basic idea in economics is that people respond to them, often in ways the designers of a rule did not intend. The results are called unintended consequences. A frequently told, if disputed, example is a bounty on pests that leads people to breed them for the payment. Others include a pay system that rewards hours instead of results, a tax on a product that shifts buying to a substitute, rent limits that many economists say can shrink rental supply, or a target for response times that leads staff to focus on measures instead of quality.

This way of thinking matters when evaluating any policy, workplace rule or platform design. Gig apps use incentives such as bonuses, surge prices and ratings, which shape when and where drivers work, and which can also push them to take risks or work longer hours than they would otherwise choose. Understanding the incentive behind a rule helps explain behavior.

In practice, ask who gains and who pays under a proposal, how people could respond, and what the rule actually measures versus what it is meant to achieve. Distinguish between the intended goal and the likely behavior. Notice the incentives of those giving you advice, including salespeople and platforms.
essays.T508:
Cognitive biases are systematic patterns in the way people judge and decide. The sunk cost fallacy is the habit of continuing something because of what has already been spent, even when the future costs outweigh the benefits. Money already paid for a repair, a course or a failing venture cannot be recovered whatever you decide, so the sensible question is what to do from here. Other common biases include loss aversion, in which a loss feels worse than an equal gain feels good; anchoring, in which a first number dominates later judgments; confirmation bias, the tendency to favor evidence that supports what you already believe; and overconfidence in one's own forecasts.

These biases matter in money decisions. People keep a costly vehicle because of what they put into it, hold on to a losing investment to avoid admitting a loss, or accept a first price as fair. A person working alone has no colleague to challenge their reasoning.

In practice, frame decisions around future costs and benefits only. Ask, if I did not already own this, would I buy it now at this price? Set a limit in advance, such as the repair cost at which you will replace a vehicle.

terms.plain: the document that sets what each government may do and who may do it
terms.quote: The Constitution defines the framework of the Federal Government of the United States.

terms.plain: Congress writes law, president carries it out, courts decide disputes
terms.quote: The Constitution of the United States divides the federal government into three branches:

terms.plain: federal, state, county, city each hold separate powers
terms.quote: The powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people.

terms.plain: sponsor, committee, floor vote (218 of 435 in the House), other chamber, president
terms.quote: If the bill passes by simple majority (218 of 435), the bill moves to the Senate.

terms.plain: numbered presidential directive to run the executive branch; not a statute, courts and Congress can undo it
terms.quote: For Executive orders issued since the start of the Clinton administration in 1993, you can now find a link to the text of the order as it appeared in the Federal Register .

terms.plain: agencies publish proposed and final rules with a comment window; rules carry the force of law
terms.quote: Federal agencies are required to publish notices of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register to enable citizens to participate in the decision making process of the Government.

terms.plain: trial, appeals, supreme; a ruling binds lower courts
terms.quote: Article III of the U.S. Constitution created the Supreme Court and authorized Congress to pass laws establishing a system of lower courts.

terms.plain: begins by statute on the first Monday in October; arguments, then opinions through early summer
terms.quote: A Term of the Supreme Court begins, by statute, on the first Monday in October.

terms.plain: you pay Social Security and Medicare yourself (self-employment tax), plus income tax, through quarterly estimates
terms.quote: Estimated tax is used to pay not only income tax, but other taxes such as self-employment tax and alternative minimum tax.

terms.plain: business miles at the IRS rate (76 cents/mile for 2026 second half)
terms.quote: If you use your car for business, charity, medical or moving purposes, you may be able to take a deduction based on the mileage used for that purpose.

terms.plain: payment-app form, sent only above $20,000 and 200 transactions; income is taxable with or without it
terms.quote: A payment app or online marketplace is required to send you a Form 1099-K if the payments you received for goods or services total over $20,000 in more than 200 transactions.

terms.plain: Congress told the Fed to seek maximum employment, stable prices, moderate long-term rates; it moves the policy rate by open market operations
terms.quote: Monetary policy in the United States comprises the Federal Reserve's actions and communications to promote maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates--the economic goals the Congress has instructed the Federal Reserve to pursue.

terms.plain: eight scheduled meetings per year
terms.quote: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings during the year and other meetings as needed.

terms.plain: lenders price off market rates that follow Fed expectations, not the policy rate directly
terms.quote: Earlier in the year, expectations of a decline in inflation and lingering concerns about stabilization in the labor market contributed to the view that the policy rate would fall further toward estimates of its long-run neutral level.
terms.term: How rates reach a car loan or mortgage

terms.plain: output, employment, and prices; each is an estimate that is later revised
terms.quote: Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA).

terms.plain: deficit is one year's overspend; debt is the running total of all deficits; interest on it is itself spending
terms.quote: The Latest Data on Federal Revenue, Spending, Deficit, and the National Debt

terms.plain: the government's checking balance, published daily
terms.quote: The Daily Treasury Statement (DTS) dataset contains a series of tables showing the daily cash and debt operations of the U.S. Treasury.

terms.plain: fiscal year starts Oct 1; no appropriation means a shutdown
terms.quote: 15 Robert Manor et al., “Federal Workers get Sent Home, Shutdown Means Job Limbo for Thousands Here,” 15 November 1995, St. Louis Dispatch : 1.A.

terms.plain: powers of the state; judicial power in Supreme Court, Court of Appeals, Circuit Courts and courts the General Assembly creates
terms.quote: The Constitution provides that the judicial power of the State is vested in a Supreme Court, a Court of Appeals, Circuit Courts and such other courts as the General Assembly may establish ( Indiana Constitution Article 7§1 ).

terms.plain: assessed value (Form 11) is the starting point, then deductions, rates, caps
terms.quote: The assessed value on the Form 11 is the starting point for calculating annual property tax payments.

terms.plain: yes/no on a measure or whether a judge stays
terms.quote: In 1970, the voters of Indiana approved a constitutional amendment providing for merit selection and retention of Indiana Supreme Court justices and Indiana Court of Appeals judges.

terms.plain: who may give, what must be reported, FEC role
